introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three and a quarter hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR QUESTIONS in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each. Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references. Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed. Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and Two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Briefly contrast the relief and drainage characteristics east and west of Easting 56 of the map area. *(5 marks)*

(ii) Using map evidence only, identify and explain the difficulties posed by the relief and drainage characteristics in the development of road network in the map area. *(6 marks)*

(iii) Suggest two strategies that can be adopted to overcome the physical challenges of road network development in the map area. *(4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to read the question.** Easting 56 is the vertical grid line labelled 56 at the bottom of the map. It divides the extract into a western part (Eastings 50 to 56) and an eastern part (Eastings 56 to 65). Use the contours, spot heights, the escarpment sign, the swamp sign and the river and stream lines of the key. Compare the two parts point by point. The observations below are read from the scan, whose quality is only medium (see the notes on uncertainty).

**(i) Contrast of relief and drainage (5 marks)**

| Feature | West of Easting 56 | East of Easting 56 |
|---|---|---|
| General height | Higher ground, spot heights generally above about 1,200 m, rising towards the western edge of the map | Lower ground, spot heights mostly about 1,150 to 1,200 m (lowest in the plain in the north-east and south-east) |
| Slope | Steep, rugged: contour lines are very closely spaced and tightly packed in many places, giving steep slopes | Gentle, undulating: contours are widely spaced, with isolated rounded hills and wide flat valley floors |
| Landforms | Ridges, spurs and deep valleys, a hachured **escarpment** near Northing 41 (about Eastings 53 to 55), steep-sided hills | A broad, almost level plain (the Ndop plain) around Ndop town and the south-east, broken by low rounded hills |
| Drainage density | High: many short streams close together, giving a dense, branching (dendritic) pattern in narrow V-shaped valleys | Lower: fewer streams, which are longer and flow in wide, shallow valleys |
| Drainage character | Fast-flowing, steep-gradient streams, probably seasonal in their upper parts, flowing down from the highland towards the plain | Slow, sluggish rivers with a low gradient (the River Noun in the east is meandering), and large areas shown with the **swampy land** sign (grey stipple) in the north-east, east and south-east |

**Conclusion.** The west is a dissected highland with steep slopes and close drainage, while the east is a lower, gentler plain, much of it poorly drained and swampy.

**(ii) Difficulties for road development (6 marks)** *(identify the problem, give the map evidence, explain the effect: about 2 marks each for three well developed points.)*
1. **Steep slopes and escarpment in the west.** Evidence: very close contours and the hachured escarpment. Explanation: gradients are too steep for straight roads; roads need cuttings, embankments and hairpin bends, which raise the construction cost and slow traffic. This is why the west has mostly earth roads and footpaths, and few settlements linked by roads.
2. **Dense, dissected drainage in the west.** Evidence: many streams cutting across the likely route. Explanation: each valley needs a bridge or a culvert, so the cost is high, and roads are often cut during heavy rain or flooded when streams rise.
3. **Swampy, waterlogged land in the east.** Evidence: the swampy land sign along the lower parts of the plain and the River Noun valley. Explanation: the soft, waterlogged ground cannot carry heavy loads without embankments and drainage, roads sink or are washed out in the rains, and roads are forced to detour round swamps along drier interfluves, which lengthens them.
4. **Rivers as barriers.** Evidence: the roads cross the River Noun at a few points only (crossing points are shown with a bridge or ford sign). Explanation: bridges are expensive and limit the number of crossing points, so roads converge on a few nodes.
5. **Result on the pattern.** The tarred road is concentrated in the more open northern part of the plain around Ndop, while the rest of the area depends on earth roads and footpaths; the road network is therefore uneven and of low density where the relief is rugged or the ground is swampy.

**(iii) Two strategies (4 marks, 2 marks each: strategy plus explanation)**
1. *Careful route alignment and engineering of the slopes:* follow the contours or the spurs and gentle ridges, use zigzags (hairpins) at the escarpment, cut and fill, and build retaining walls and side drains and plant grass or trees on cuttings, so that the gradient stays gentle and the roads are stable.
2. *Bridges, culverts and raised, drained road beds across the wet lowlands:* build bridges at the valleys, culverts on small streams and raised embankments with side ditches across the swamps, then gravel or tar the roads so that they remain open throughout the year.

Other acceptable strategies: use of local labour and community road maintenance, building feeder roads from the existing tarred road, and use of cheaper all-weather surfaces.

**(i) Irrigation and hydro-electric power (4 marks, 2 marks for each)**

*Irrigation farming - good possibility.*
- Evidence: the extensive flat, low-lying plain in the east and south-east with the **swampy land** sign, a permanent **river** (River Noun) with many tributary streams, and a **rice plantation** sign in the plain.
- The gentle slopes allow water to be led in small canals (gravity irrigation) and to be stored in the wet season; the many streams and the river supply water all year round, so the dry-season crops can be irrigated.

*Hydro-electric power - limited, mostly small-scale.*
- Evidence: in the west the many streams descend a steep slope (close contours, escarpment), so the head of water is high, but the streams are short and small, so the volume is small: only mini or micro hydro is likely.
- In the east the Noun has a gentle gradient and a wide flat valley: little head, so a large dam would flood a very wide area (farmland, settlement) for a small output.
- Conclusion: the area is better suited to irrigation than to large hydro-electric production.

**(ii) Two physical problems and two solutions (6 marks: 1 mark per problem, 1 mark per explanation, 1 mark per solution)**

| Physical problem (with map evidence) | Solution |
|---|---|
| **Flooding and waterlogging.** The rice fields lie on low swampy land beside the river, which floods in the rains and drowns the young crop or delays planting. | Build drainage and diversion canals and dykes (embankments) along the river, and control the water level in the paddies; plant flood-tolerant, short-cycle rice varieties. |
| **Water shortage in the dry season.** Many of the minor streams are shown as intermittent streams (dashed) so that irrigation water is not available all year in the upper parts. | Build small dams or retention ponds and irrigation canals from the permanent river; use pumps, and stagger the planting dates. |

Other acceptable problems: poor drainage and acid or peaty swamp soils (solution: liming and organic manure), steep slopes on the margins that cause erosion and silting of the fields (solution: terracing, contour bunds and afforestation on the slopes).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Calculate the sinuosity index of the river Noun located north of the map from 631440 to 646400. *(4 marks)*

(ii) State the significance of your result or answer. *(2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sinuosity index (4 marks)**

*Formula.* The sinuosity index (SI) compares the real length of the channel with the straight-line distance between the same two points:

$$SI = \frac{\text{actual channel length}}{\text{straight-line distance}}$$

*Step 1 - Locate the points (1 mark).* Grid reference 631440 means Easting 63.1 and Northing 44.0 (63 and a tenth, 44.0), and 646400 means Easting 64.6 and Northing 40.0. The first point lies on the River Noun near the top of the map, where the river is labelled; the second lies where the river reaches the south-eastern part of the Ndop plain.

*Step 2 - Straight-line distance (1 mark).* Difference in Easting = 64.6 - 63.1 = 1.5 km; difference in Northing = 44.0 - 40.0 = 4.0 km. By Pythagoras (or a ruler between the two points):

$$d = \sqrt{1.5^2 + 4.0^2} = \sqrt{18.25} \approx 4.3\ \text{km}$$

*Step 3 - Actual channel length (1 mark).* Lay a piece of string or the edge of a paper strip along every bend of the river from 631440 to 646400, mark the two points, straighten it and measure it on the scale (1 km = 2 cm at 1:50,000; on a reduced copy use the 1 km grid squares instead). Tracing the course on the extract gives a channel length of about **5.5 km** (a candidate's measure of 5.3 to 5.6 km is acceptable).

*Step 4 - Calculation (1 mark).*

$$SI = \frac{5.5}{4.3} \approx 1.3$$

(For 5.4 km the result is 1.26; for 5.6 km it is 1.30. The answer is therefore about **1.3**.)

**(ii) Significance (2 marks)**
- A sinuosity index of 1.0 means a perfectly straight channel; the further above 1, the more bends. A commonly used classification: below about 1.05 straight, about 1.05 to 1.5 sinuous, above about 1.5 meandering. A value of about 1.3 shows that the River Noun is **sinuous (moderately meandering)** in this stretch. *(1 mark)*
- This indicates a **low gradient** river flowing over a flat plain (the Ndop plain): it has little energy to erode downwards, so it swings from side to side, eroding the outer banks and depositing on the inner banks. Such a channel is slow, floods its banks easily, and leaves swamps and oxbow features, which is consistent with the swampy land on the map. It also means the river is about 28 per cent longer than a straight line would be, which is useful for irrigation and fishing but unsuitable for hydro-electric power. *(1 mark)*
